source_caption:
🎬 Junior (1994)

Junior follows Dr. Alex Hesse, a brilliant but emotionally reserved scientist who has dedicated his career to developing a revolutionary fertility drug designed to help women maintain healthy pregnancies. Working alongside his enthusiastic research partner, Dr. Larry Arbogast, Alex faces a major setback when their experimental project loses its funding and permission to continue human trials. Desperate to prove that their discovery works, Larry convinces Alex to participate in an extraordinary experiment by becoming pregnant himself. What begins as a scientific test quickly turns into a hilarious and unpredictable adventure as Alex experiences the physical and emotional changes of pregnancy firsthand. From unexpected cravings and mood swings to embarrassing situations, complicated medical appointments, and increasingly difficult attempts to hide his condition, Alex discovers that carrying a child is far more challenging than he ever imagined. Meanwhile, his growing connection with fellow scientist Dr. Diana Reddin adds another layer of confusion to his already unusual circumstances. As the pregnancy progresses, Alex begins developing feelings and responsibilities he never expected, forcing him to reconsider his priorities and understanding of family. Combining outrageous comedy, heartfelt moments, and an imaginative scientific premise, the film explores parenthood, friendship, love, responsibility, and the surprising ways life can change when least expected.

🎭 Genre: Comedy • Romance • Sci-Fi

⭐ IMDb: 4.7/10

⏱️ Runtime: 1h 49m • PG-13

🎥 Director: Ivan Reitman

source_details.synopsis: Junior is a 1994 American science fiction comedy film directed and produced by Ivan Reitman, and starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, Danny DeVito and Emma Thompson. The film follows Alex Hesse, an Austrian-American scientist who agrees to undergo a male pregnancy from a newly developed drug Expectane. The film marked the third and last collaboration for Reitman and Schwarzenegger, succeeding Twins (1988) and Kindergarten Cop (1990), as well as the second and last collaboration for DeVito, Reitman, and Schwarzenegger, succeeding Twins.
